title: Indian lead recycler Gravita gets go-ahead to launch US subsidiary – Batteries International
content: India-based Gravita is set to expand its global operations by entering the US market, the lead battery recycler confirmed in a surprise announcement. Gravita’s board gave the green light for proposals to establish a wholly owned subsidiary stateside on October 5. The move comes just weeks after Batteries International revealed Indian lead battery manufacturing giant, Amara Raja Energy & Mobility, had incorporated a subsidiary in the US. Gravita’s proposed operation, initially dubbed ‘Gravita Recyclers USA’, has yet to be formally incorporated. Initial capital is expected to be $50,000, although a schedule for starting up the unit has not been disclosed. The group said in a filing with the National Stock Exchange of India that the proposed business would be engaged in the trading of scrap and scrap materials but did not give a detailed breakdown of proposed operations. The move follows months of capacity expansion projects across the group’s recycling sites in India, which Gravita said were designed to boost operational efficiencies, optimise logistics and better serve key export markets. The lead recycling major also has a fledgling lithium recycling operation, set up alongside lead processing activities at its Mundra plant in Gujurat. Batteries International reported earlier this year that Gravita had further extended its presence in the copper and copper alloy products market by acquiring a 98.5% stake in India’s Rashtriya Metal Industries. Beyond India, the group has grown into a diversified, multi-material recycling group with operations across Asia, Africa and Europe since being established in 1992. In May 2026, Gravita posted adjusted consolidated EBITDA of Rs 452 crore ($47 million) for the fiscal year ended in March 2026 ― aided by a slight growth in lead sales. The lead recycler reported a 7% increase in sales in the lead segment of its business, amounting to 49,000 tonnes per annum in fiscal 2026. title: South 8 Technologies Signs 3-Year Supply Agreement with Galvion to Power Arctic SoloPack - Batteries News
content:
South 8 Technologies Signs 3-Year Supply Agreement with Galvion to Power Arctic SoloPack
SAN DIEGO–(BUSINESS WIRE)–
South 8 Technologies
, a U.S. manufacturer of lithium-ion battery cells for extreme environments, has signed a multi-year master supply agreement with Galvion, a defense technology company specializing in integrated head systems and soldier power and data solutions. South 8’s AE35 cell will power SoloPack™ Arctic, Galvion’s new extreme cold weather soldier power solution that will make its debut at AUSA 2026 in Washington, D.C., October 12–14
The agreement converts a
Letter of Intent
signed by the companies in July 2025 into a commercial supply framework and marks another step in South 8’s transition from technology development to scaled production and customer delivery.
The agreement comes as South 8 moves its ARCTIC™ AE35 18650 cell into commercial production at its San Diego headquarters. The company’s new manufacturing line has begun production, scaling toward 5 MWh of annual production capacity in 2027, equivalent to approximately 450,000 AE35 cells per year.
The AE35 is South 8’s first high volume 18650 cell. Powered by the company’s proprietary LiGas® electrolyte technology, the AE35 will charge and discharge from −60 °C to +60 °C (−76 °F to +140 °F) and uses the familiar 18650 form factor. Cells will be produced at South 8’s San Diego facility, providing customers with a domestically manufactured battery cell and a defined pathway toward meeting applicable National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) sourcing requirements once those rules are finalized.
Jungwoo Lee,
CEO of South 8 Technologies, said:
Partnering with Galvion to bring LiGas technology into the field is an important commercialization milestone,
“This multi-year supply agreement demonstrates that our technology is moving beyond development and into mission-critical applications where reliable power in extreme cold can make a real difference. Galvion’s proven SoloPack platform is an ideal application for AE35, and we’re proud to help deliver the performance and resilience warfighters need in the world’s most demanding environments.”
SoloPack Arctic extends Galvion’s soldier power portfolio into extreme cold environments at a time of increasing focus on Arctic readiness. As the system advances toward broader deployment, evaluation of SoloPack Arctic will be happening in field exercises in Alaska, where reliable power in extreme cold is a critical operational requirement.
Jonathan Blanshay,
Founder and Executive Chairman of Galvion, said:
When we began working with South 8, we saw an opportunity to combine their innovative cell technology with our proven SoloPack battery to address a very real challenge for operations in extreme cold,
“SoloPack Arctic is the result of that collaboration, and this agreement marks an important next step as we move from development into field evaluation and commercialization.” For South 8, SoloPack Arctic represents the next stage of commercialization: bringing the AE35 into production, seeing the cell integrated into a customer product, and converting an earlier LOI into a commercial supply agreement supporting market launch.

title: Rimac Technology and ECOBLOX Partner to Bring Rimac Battery and Power Electronics Technology to AI Data Centers - Batteries News
content:
Rimac Technology and ECOBLOX Partner to Bring Rimac Battery and Power Electronics Technology to AI Data Centers
ZAGREB, CROATIA and DUBAI, UAE – October 7, 2026
Rimac Technology
, an EV technology company specializing in battery, powertrain and electronic systems, and
, a global innovator in AI compute infrastructure, announced today a Joint Development Agreement to deliver a state-of-the-art Modular Data Center (MDC) solution. The joint offering integrates Rimac Technology’s battery and power electronics technology with ECOBLOX’s AI infrastructure, MDC architecture, design and hardware/software system integration.
As AI and high-performance computing drive demand for significantly more computing power, the availability of energy, cooling capacity and suitable deployment space is becoming increasingly important for data center development. The joint solution addresses these challenges in a compact, integrated architecture built for high-density workloads.
A Modular Architecture for AI Infrastructure
Rimac Technology is leveraging over a decade of high-voltage engineering expertise to develop next-generation power solutions, as AI compute transitions towards 400 VDC and 800 VDC architectures. Partnering with ECOBLOX, the two companies are engineering high-density modular solutions tailored to the demanding power requirements of AI compute.
The joint Modular Data Center integrates Rimac Technology UNI battery modules, streamlining serviceability, and enabling longer continuous backup power for critical computing hardware. Its Battery Management System (BMS) delivers real-time monitoring and control, streaming core telemetry directly into the ECOBLOX Data Center Infrastructure Management (DCIM) platform for centralized visibility, automated alarms and analytics, while power conversion, UPS, precision cooling and IT infrastructure are unified within a single, modular footprint.
Proven Technologies, Combined for AI Infrastructure
Developed to strict automotive standards, Rimac Technology UNI battery modules combine high-performance density, compact packaging, built-in safety and advanced thermal management in a high-volume industrialized battery solution. They are designed for use across automotive, energy storage, marine, off-highway, commercial and industrial applications, and now AI infrastructure.
As an NVIDIA Preferred Partner, ECOBLOX delivers complete, end-to-end AI infrastructure — from high-density factory-engineered Modular Data Centers (MDCs) to full GPU system integration, encompassing cluster design, procurement, installation, and managed service operations. By pairing advanced air- and liquid-cooled pre-fab enclosures with its proprietary DCIM and HPC/GPUaaS software stacks, ECOBLOX enables cloud providers, enterprises, and sovereign entities to deploy turnkey, exascale-ready compute directly at local power sources in just 6 to 8 months.
Doug Makishima
Chief Executive Officer, ECOBLOX, said:
Partnering with Rimac Technology allows us to redefine high-density power delivery for the next generation of AI compute.
Nurdin Pitarević
,Chief Executive Officer, Rimac Technology, said:
Our battery and power electronics technologies have been developed and industrialized to meet some of the most demanding requirements in the automotive industry.
The same capabilities are increasingly relevant to high-power AI infrastructure, where power density, thermal management, safety and reliability are critical. Together with ECOBLOX, we are applying these technologies to a new high-power application and bringing automotive-grade technology to AI data centers.
The completed modular data center is on track for installation at the Rimac Campus, nearby Zagreb, Croatia in November 2026, where it will serve as a live demonstration of the joint solution and a platform for customer and partner engagement.

title: Volt Harbor to Showcase Software-Defined Energy Platform at The Battery Show North America 2026 - Batteries News
content:
Volt Harbor to Showcase Software-Defined Energy Platform at The Battery Show North America 2026
The company will demonstrate MAC-BESS™, its battery-agnostic technology that cuts battery project costs by half and optimizes how power flows through data centers and the grid
ANN ARBOR, Mich., October 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ —
Volt Harbor
, the Ann Arbor–based software-defined energy startup that
publicly launched in May
, will exhibit at
The Battery Show North America 2026
hosted at Huntington Place in Detroit, October 12–15. Volt Harbor will be at Booth #6212, demonstrating how its MAC-BESS™ platform is a solution for the entire front-end power stack, from the grid to the data center, in a single battery-agnostic system.
Grid resilience depends less on how much storage gets built than on how intelligently power moves through it, and the layer with the most untapped potential is the power electronics. Unlike traditional energy infrastructure, which requires expensive hardware overhauls to adapt to new needs, Volt Harbor’s platform uses software changes to adapt Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) dynamically. This supports any input or output, including new battery chemistries and “second-life” EV batteries, inside a single unified system. The result is roughly 40-50% lower capital and operating costs, 50% less physical footprint, and ultrafast energy response with no single point of failure.
This year’s Battery Show comes at a pivotal moment for storage project economics. Today, a storage project is a fifteen-year asset bought through a day-one procurement process, and the architecture chosen determines almost everything that follows. Systems that manage their batteries as a single block age at the pace of their worst modules. This is why most projects that hold up, and those that get written down, were effectively decided long before commissioning. MAC-BESS™ takes a different approach: it manages every battery module independently, extending usable life while needing fewer batteries and letting operators augment or replace with whatever supply is available at the time, and making units swappable without taking the system offline.
Dr. Al-Thaddeus Avestruz,
CEO of Volt Harbor, said:
The Battery Show is where the people actually building the next generation of battery supply, infrastructure, and end-use storage systems come together, which makes us excited to be on the show floor,
“The industry has spent a decade optimizing the batteries themselves. The layer that almost nobody has really touched is the power electronics architecture, and that is where the next step-change in cost, flexibility, and project life actually comes from.”
Volt Harbor’s platform is deploying a utility pilot in 2027 with DTE Energy, Michigan’s largest utility, where second-life EV batteries will buffer high-power EV charging events that exceed local grid capacity. The same architecture is being readied for data center deployments, where AI loads swing energy facilities from 30% to full rated capacity within milliseconds and back. The legacy power stack was never designed to absorb this pattern, and it’s part of why grid interconnection queues in major data center markets now run past four years. Storage and power electronics that absorb those spikes let the grid supply the average, which means more compute for every megawatt of existing interconnection, or a smaller interconnection that clears the queue sooner.

title: NMG Develops Low-carbon-Footprint Anode Material Coating Process in Collaboration with McGill University - Batteries News
content:
NMG Develops Low-carbon-Footprint Anode Material Coating Process in Collaboration with McGill University
MONTRÉAL–(BUSINESS WIRE)–Nouveau Monde Graphite Inc. (“NMG” or the “Company”) (
FSE: NM9A
) announces the development, in collaboration with a research team from McGill University, of a new green-chemistry coating process for anode materials that offers the potential to improve the carbon profile of manufacturing while meeting industry performance requirements. This solution reduces the carbon footprint associated with coating, uses readily available raw materials, and remains compatible with existing manufacturing equipment.
Eric Desaulniers,
Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer of NMG, said:
I am very proud of the work accomplished by our R&D team and of this successful collaboration with McGill University, a world-renowned institution, to develop this new coating process for anode materials,
“This innovation, together with our ongoing investments in R&D, reflects our commitment to continuously improving our processes and products in order to deliver an ever-stronger value proposition to our present and future customers. It also aligns with our objective of developing sustainable and resilient supply chains that are less dependent on petroleum-derived products and sheltered from the volatility of their costs.”
This process was developed through a collaboration between NMG and a McGill University research team, under a partnership that began in 2020 to advance low environmental footprint battery material technologies. The work was carried out under the supervision of Professor Philippe Ouzilleau, with contributions from Professors Changhong Cao, Raynald Gauvin, Jinhyuk Lee, Sidney Omelon and Sylvain Coulombe. Professor Philippe Ouzilleau specializes in metallurgical engineering and materials science and is recognized for his expertise in the processing of carbon-based materials and the development of industrial processes with a lower environmental footprint for the metallurgy, advanced materials, and energy sectors.
Under the terms of the agreement, Nouveau Monde Graphite benefits from commercial exclusivity for any future use of this technology. The research project was initially funded through the Québec government’s Mining Research and Innovation Support Program (PARIDM), and subsequently through a grant from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC).
According to our estimates, replacing a pitch coating, the industry standard, with a bio-based coating could substantially reduce Scope 1 CO₂e emissions by 130 kg per tonne of coated spherical purified graphite (CSPG) produced. This estimate relates to direct emissions and does not, at this stage, constitute an assessment of the product’s full life cycle carbon footprint. The team is continuing its work to further reduce Scope 2 and Scope 3 CO₂e emissions. Electrochemical testing was conducted in accordance with the protocol of a leading cell manufacturer, and our results demonstrate equivalent performance in terms of capacity, first-cycle efficiency, and fast charging. Given the promising results achieved at the laboratory scale, the next steps toward the industrialization of this innovative technology, for which a patent application has been filed, will include comparative long-term cycling tests, the evaluation of new material types, and, ultimately, a validation campaign on industrial-scale equipment.
This collaboration with McGill University illustrates the role applied research and process innovation play in NMG’s strategy to develop one of the first fully integrated natural graphite production platforms in the G7. As construction at the Matawinie Mine is underway and a final investment decision for the 13ktpy Bécancour Battery Material Plant is targeted in the upcoming months, the Company pursues the advancement of its integrated value chain while continuously enhancing the performance, sustainability and competitiveness of its future products.
This innovation in anode material coating will be among the topics covered by the NMG team at The Battery Show North America in Detroit next week (booth 4638). During the event, the Company will meet with industry leaders, customers, and partners to discuss the progress of its vertically integrated strategy, as well as its product portfolio, its R&D projects and opportunities to strengthen the North American supply chain through new strategic collaborations.

title: Fraunhofer ZESS strengthens technology transfer and sustainable energy storage research in Germany - Batteries News
content:
Fraunhofer ZESS strengthens technology transfer and sustainable energy storage research in Germany
At a ceremony on October 5, 2026, the Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft officially opened the new building of the Fraunhofer Center for Energy Storage and Systems ZESS in Braunschweig. The German federal government and the State of Lower Saxony have invested approximately 49.85 million euros in the research facility. Covering around 3,300 square meters – including ap-proximately 1,750 square meters of laboratory space and a 450-square-meter drying room – it provides researchers with state-of-the-art infrastructure for the development of next-generation solid-state batteries and innovative hydrogen technologies.
In his welcome address to the around 100 guests from the worlds of politics, business, and science, Prof. Constantin Häfner, Executive Board Member for Research and Transfer at the Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft, emphasized the strategic importance of the new center within the Fraunhofer research landscape: “High-performance battery and hydrogen technologies are crucial to the energy and mobility transition – and to the competitiveness of our industry. With the Fraunhofer ZESS, we are turning inventions into industrial innovations, thereby strengthening value creation and technological sovereignty in Germany and Europe.”
Federal Minister of Research Dorothee Bär praised
the center as a key building block for Germany’s innovative capacity:
The development of high-performance battery and hydrogen technologies will play a decisive role in determining how competitive and self-reliant Germany and Europe will be in the coming decades.
”With the Fraunhofer ZESS, we are making a targeted investment in a research infrastructure that combines cutting-edge research with industrial implementation. This strengthens Germany’s international position in key technology fields, fully in line with our High-Tech Agenda for Germany.”
Lower Saxony’s Minister of Science,
Falko Mohrs
, also emphasized the strategic importance of the new center:
In Lower Saxony, we are making a targeted commitment to future technologies that secure value creation, innovation, and skilled jobs.
”The investment in the Fraunhofer ZESS is an excellent example of this. The new location complements Lower Saxony’s battery and hydrogen ecosystem and creates ideal conditions for translating research results into industrial applications more quickly. As a result, we are establishing excellent conditions for science, technology transfer, and economic development.”
Prof. Anja Hesse
, Head of the Department of Culture and Science for the City of Braunschweig, emphasized:
The Fraunhofer ZESS exemplifies the innovative strength of the Braunschweig region, which ranks among Europe’s leading research regions.
”The new research facility provides a significant boost to Braunschweig as a hub for science and innovation and transmits a strong signal regarding our region’s future viability.”
Prof. Angela Ittel, President of the Technische Universität Braunschweig, added: “With the Fraunhofer ZESS, our internationally renowned battery research gains a strong partner on the path to industrial application. Together with our Battery LabFactory and the Center for Circular Production of Next Batteries and Fuel Cells (CPC), we will advance resource-efficient technologies that will benefit us here in the region – and far beyond.”
Prof. Christoph Herrmann,
Institute Director of the Fraunhofer IST and spokesperson for the Fraunhofer ZESS, also emphasized the close collaboration with the TU Braunschweig, within the Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft, and with industry partners:
At the Fraunhofer ZESS, we consider the entire process chain – from new materials, through production technologies, and on to sustainability and the circular economy.
”By pooling complementary expertise, we create ideal conditions for the targeted further development of key technologies – such as solid-state batteries and hydrogen technologies – for industrial scaling and application.”
During a panel discussion, experts discussed the future prospects of battery and hydrogen technologies. They emphasized that scientific excellence across the entire value chain, speed in development and technology transfer, and consideration of economic and environmental conditions are key factors for success.
The combination of technological innovation and sustainability is one of the guiding principles at the Fraunhofer ZESS. This applies not only to the research work, facilities, and equipment, but also to the building itself. Guests were able to experience this for themselves during the subsequent tour. The research building was constructed as a hybrid timber structure with minimal use of concrete. Photovoltaic systems on the roof and façade, green roofs, an energy-efficient building design, and flexible research spaces combine state-of-the-art research conditions with a holistic approach to sustainability. The open hall structure also allows for long-term adaptation to future research requirements, making the building a forward-looking and resource-efficient research facility.

title: Duracell Opens New $56 Million Global Innovation Center for Research and Development in Atlanta’s Science Square - Batteries News
content:
Duracell Opens New $56 Million Global Innovation Center for Research and Development in Atlanta’s Science Square
ATLANTA–(BUSINESS WIRE)–Duracell, one of the world’s leading battery manufacturers, today officially opened its new Global Innovation Center for Research and Development at Science Square Labs in Atlanta. Representing an investment of $56 million, the 83,000-square-foot facility is expected to create 120 jobs and serve as the central anchor for the company’s global battery technology innovation network.
Representatives from the State of Georgia, the City of Atlanta and Georgia Tech joined Duracell at Science Square this morning for a ceremonial ribbon cutting to celebrate the opening. The ceremony highlighted a shared vision for economic growth, local talent recruitment, and statewide technological advancement.
Roberto Mendez,
Chief Executive Officer at Duracell, said:
Georgia has been a vital home for Duracell for decades, and expanding our footprint into Science Square was a natural next step in that partnership,
“By positioning our teams within a thriving innovation ecosystem, we are giving our world-class R+D organization the platform, technology and collaborative environment they need to power the future.”
Adjacent to Georgia Tech at 101 Nerem Street NW, the new facility unites scientists, engineers, and cross-functional teams to accelerate battery innovation from concept to commercialization. Positioned on Atlanta’s West Midtown, the center bridges academic talent with corporate R&D, directly linking Duracell’s LaGrange manufacturing plant and Fairburn distribution center into a cohesive end-to-end state network.
Liben Hailu,
Chief Technology Officer at Duracell, said:
The strategic placement of our new facility allows us to tap into a rich pipeline of diverse talent coming from Georgia Tech and neighboring research institutions,
“We look forward to welcoming the next generation of scientists and engineers to the Duracell team as we push the boundaries of energy technology right here in Atlanta.”
Duracell’s new global research and development headquarters was developed by Trammell Crow Company in partnership with Georgia Advanced Technology Ventures, an affiliate of Georgia Tech. Partners Real Estate represented Duracell in the transaction, while CBRE represented Trammell Crow Company. The complex tenant fit-out was executed by a specialized design and construction team including Perkins&Will, AHA Consulting Engineers, Walter P Moore and Brasfield & Gorrie.
Brasfield & Gorrie
Vice President and Division Manager Scott Cooper, said:
An R&D lab build-out of this scale touches nearly every system in a building and requires every one of them to be exactly right,
“From specialized dry room systems to relocating hundreds of pieces of owner-furnished equipment across floors, the complexity was real. This kind of space directly supports Duracell’s work in Atlanta and beyond, and we’re glad our team could deliver that for them.”

title: The Wait Is Over: AuroraCell RESS Now in Stock in Poland - Batteries News
content:
The Wait Is Over: AuroraCell RESS Now in Stock in Poland
After a long wait, we are delighted to announce that AuroraCell Residential Energy Storage Systems are now in stock at our warehouse in Poland. Our sodium-ion RESS is here, bringing long-life energy storage closer to European homes and installation partners.
Thank you to everyone who has followed the development, asked questions and waited for this arrival. Having stock in Poland is an important step: homeowners, installers and distributors can now talk to us about a system from the available batch and plan their next project with our team.
Why NCO is ideal for residential energy storage
A home battery works quietly in the background, storing energy and releasing it when the household needs it. That makes
durability, daily cycling and safety
central to the choice. Sodium Chromoxide (NCO), the sodium-ion chemistry behind AuroraCell RESS, is a strong fit for exactly these priorities.
Built for years of everyday energy storage
Residential storage should be considered over decades. With an expected service life of
25–30 years

POSCO Future M signs KRW 1,1 trillion LFP Cathode Material Supply Contract with SK On
POSCO Future M (CEO EOM Gi Chen) has signed a large-scale supply contract with SK On for LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cathode materials.
Hard on the heels of last month’s long-term agreement to supply 190,000 tons of LFP cathode materials to a Korean battery maker, the company has now secured another major contract as it moves into the LFP market in earnest.
POSCO Future M has been working with SK On as a supplier of anode materials and plans to strengthen the partnership further through this contract, its first to supply SK On with cathode materials. The contract also means POSCO Future M now supplies cathode and anode materials to all three Korean battery makers, broadening its customer portfolio and putting its mid- to long-term growth on an even firmer foundation.
The contract, signed on the 22nd, is worth approximately KRW 1.1 trillion over three years, from 2027 through 2029, and can be extended by an additional two years upon agreement between the two companies.
While LFP batteries have lower power output than ternary batteries such as NCM (nickel-cobalt-manganese) and NCA (nickel-cobalt-aluminum), their strengths lie in competitive pricing and a long lifespan. With power demand recently surging due to the build-out of AI data centers, among other factors, demand for LFP batteries used in ESS is growing to ensure a stable power supply. LFP batteries are also increasingly being adopted in the electric vehicle market, particularly in entry-level models.
POSCO Future M is actively responding to customer demand by adding LFP cathode materials to its existing portfolio centered on ternary (NCM and NCA) materials. The company recently completed converting part of its high-nickel cathode material production lines at the Pohang plant to LFP cathode material production, and is set to begin mass-production supply from the end of this year. POSCO Future M plans to continue expanding production capacity by converting more lines as further orders come in.
Going forward, the company also plans to produce and supply LFP cathode materials with further improved cost competitiveness and quality by applying a new process that uses lithium from salt lakes in Argentina, drawing on raw material supply chain cooperation across POSCO group.
POSCO Future M continues to hold discussions with major battery makers and automakers on supplying cathode and anode materials, backed by a diverse product portfolio and by a supply chain and technological capabilities that can navigate global trade regulations. The company is also stepping up the expansion of its production capacity. Its moves include a KRW 1 trillion long-term supply contract for synthetic graphite anode materials, signed with a global automaker in March this year, and plans to invest approximately KRW 357 billion in a new synthetic graphite anode material plant in Vietnam. A plant to process spherical graphite, an intermediate material for natural graphite anode materials, is under construction at the Saemangeum National Industrial Complex in Jeonbuk and is scheduled to begin trial operation in early 2027, with completion and full-scale mass production planned for the second half of the year.
In July, POSCO group announced its future growth strategy, outlining a vision to build a Triple-Core system and become a “national supplier of critical resources.” The system spans industrial resources (steel), strategic resources (such as lithium, cathode and anode materials, and rare earths), and energy resources (LNG and renewable energy).
In line with this strategy, POSCO Future M aims to build on its unrivaled technology to strengthen its business competitiveness and expand its markets, and to emerge as a global leader in the cathode and anode materials business, one of the pillars of the group’s strategic resources.

Could You Pass a Battery Safety Test? New Quiz Challenges Americans’ Charging Habits During Fire Prevention Week (Oct. 4 – 10)
Cirba Solutions’ free Battery Smarts Quiz turns national consumer research into 10 questions to boost battery safety awareness
CHARLOTTE, N.C., Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — The average American owns 11 products powered by lithium batteries. Most people use one every day, but few were taught how to properly charge, store or dispose of them safely. To close that gap, Cirba Solutions, the leading battery recycling materials and management company in North America, today launched the Battery Smarts Quiz, a free online tool that helps people test and improve their battery safety knowledge in minutes.
The launch comes during Fire Prevention Week™ (Oct. 4-10), hosted each year by the National Fire Protection Association (
). This year’s theme, “Charge Into Fire Safety™. Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” focuses on the everyday charging habits that help keep homes and communities safe.
The quiz builds directly on The Missing Link: Consumer Awareness in the Battery Life Cycle, the consumer study Cirba Solutions released earlier this year as a follow-up to its 2024 research. The study found that 91 percent of Americans would recycle their lithium batteries if it were as easy as throwing them away, but most responded that they do not know how or where.
Karen Gay,
Community Engagement Manager at Cirba Solutions, said:
Our research told us exactly where the knowledge gaps are, so we built the quiz around them,
“We wanted it to feel less like a lecture and more like a safety challenge you want to share with your friends and family – a fun way to gain knowledge around something most of us do every day. If someone walks away knowing to charge their e-bike away from the front door, or to tape the terminals of a used battery before recycling it instead of tossing it in the trash, that’s a win for their household and their community.”
In 10 questions, the quiz covers the moments that matter most:
Choosing a charger:
why the right charger matters.
Where to charge:
the best spots for phones, laptops, e-bikes, e-scooters, etc.
When to unplug:
how long devices should stay on the charger.
Warning signs:
what to do if a battery gets hot or swells.
Disposal:
how to get rid of end-of-life batteries safely.
Recycling know-how:
what can be recycled and how American consumers stack up.
Each answer includes a short explanation of why it matters. At the end, users get a result ranging from “Champion Charger” to “Reset Required,” plus a shareable card to post across multiple platforms and challenge friends and family.
The quiz expands on #BatterySmarts, Cirba Solutions’ ongoing social media series in which employees answer common battery safety and recycling questions and brings those lessons together in one place for anyone to take and share. It’s also the latest resource from SustainABILITY 10,000, the company’s commitment to 10,000 hours of community engagement and education across North America, and supports the initiative’s Digital Advocacy pillar, which focuses on online tools that any community can use.

title: New battery chemistry could help lithium-sulfur batteries store more energy - Batteries News
content:
New battery chemistry could help lithium-sulfur batteries store more energy
Lithium-sulfur batteries are an experimental alternative to today’s lithium-ion batteries that could store considerably more energy for their weight but have proved difficult to make durable and practical.
Now, researchers at Vanderbilt University and the University of Maryland have demonstrated a new approach that could push their energy-storage potential further.
In a study published in
Nature Energy
, the team developed a battery chemistry that allows sulfur to participate in an additional energy-storing reaction. The result is a sulfur-based battery that operates at a higher average voltage while also storing more charge.
De-en Jiang,
the H, said:
The traditional way of thinking about lithium-sulfur batteries leaves some of sulfur’s redox power untapped,
Eugene McBrayer Professor of Chemical Engineering and Professor of Chemistry. He is also a co-corresponding author of the study. “We wanted to see whether we could expand sulfur’s redox capability and use it to store more energy.”
Getting more energy out of sulfur
Sulfur has long attracted battery researchers because of its abundance and lower cost. Plus, it can store far more charge by weight than the materials commonly used in lithium-ion battery cathodes.
The challenge has been that most lithium-sulfur batteries operate at a relatively low voltage. And the amount of energy a battery can store depends on both how much charge it holds and the voltage at which it operates.
The researchers found a way to improve both functions. In a conventional lithium-sulfur battery, each sulfur atom can exchange two electrons as the battery charges and discharges. The new system extends that chemistry by introducing chlorine, allowing sulfur to exchange a third electron.
That additional reaction also takes place at a higher voltage. In laboratory tests, the new chemistry increased sulfur’s charge-storage capacity by about 58% and raised the battery’s average operating voltage from about 2.05 volts to 2.54 volts compared with standard lithium-sulfur chemistry tested under the same conditions. The combination of the higher charge-storage capacity and the higher voltage allowed one kilogram of sulfur to store more than 1,700 watt-hours of energy in their experimental cell.
Designing an electrolyte to make it work
Making the new reaction reversible presented another challenge. The team needed chlorine to interact with sulfur during charging without allowing the resulting sulfur-chlorine compound to travel through the battery and react with its lithium-metal electrode.
Researchers used molecular simulations to understand how lithium and chloride ions behave inside different electrolytes. Those calculations led to the design of an electrolyte in which chloride remains available to react with sulfur.
The team also selected an electrolyte in which the sulfur-chlorine reaction product does not readily dissolve. That helps keep it where it belongs—inside the battery’s positive electrode—so the reaction can be reversed when the battery discharges.
Experiments using several different spectroscopy techniques confirmed that sulfur repeatedly moved through the newly accessible chemical state as the cells were charged and discharged.
An early demonstration
The researchers ultimately built a small, single-layer pouch cell to show that the chemistry could work outside the coin cells commonly used for early battery experiments. The pouch cell retained 78% of its initial capacity after 100 charging cycles.
Considerable work remains before the approach could be used commercially. The prototype uses a lithium-metal electrode, relatively modest amounts of sulfur and more electrolyte than would be desirable in a commercial battery.
But Jiang said the larger significance is the possibility of expanding the chemistry available to sulfur batteries rather than simply improving the conventional reaction.
The researchers estimate that, after accounting for major battery components rather than the electrode alone, the approach could enable a stack-level specific energy of 477 watt-hours per kilogram, about 37% higher than the conventional lithium-sulfur system used for comparison in the study.

content:
Fraunhofer Battery Alliance and South Korean Partners Reaffirm Expansion of Their Collaboration in Battery Research
Münster continues to emerge as an international hub for battery research: At Fraunhofer FFB, the Fraunhofer Battery Alliance, along with the Korea Environment Corporation (K-eco), Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), and the city of Pohang, signed two Memorandums of Understanding to deepen their collaboration. The signing took place during a visit by the South Korean delegation to Münster. The goal is to collaborate more closely on the development of new battery technologies, production processes, and recycling solutions.
Münster.
As the demand for batteries grows, so do the requirements for their manufacturing and recycling. New technologies must not only be developed but also made viable for industrial use. The Fraunhofer Battery Alliance and its South Korean partners therefore intend to pool their expertise and advance joint research and development activities.
Prof. Dr. Jens Tübke, director of the Fraunhofer FFB and spokesperson for the Fraunhofer Battery Alliance, welcomes the collaboration: “The development of new battery technologies and the establishment of a sustainable battery value chain require close cooperation between research and industry across national borders. Together with our South Korean partners, we aim to pool scientific expertise and jointly develop solutions for battery cell manufacturing and recycling. The two agreements provide an important foundation for deepening technical exchange and launching joint research activities.”
Joint Research Along the Battery Value Chain
At a seminar, the partners exchanged information about their research activities and discussed concrete approaches for future joint projects:
The memorandums of understanding identify potential research areas with POSTECH and the City of Pohang, ranging from materials for lithium-ion batteries and next-generation batteries to cell and production technologies, as well as recycling and the circular economy . The City of Pohang intends to provide administrative and funding support for joint activities with local companies as well as international research collaborations.
With K-eco, the focus is primarily on the recycling of used batteries as well as certification and quality assurance procedures for recovered battery materials. In addition, the partners intend to explore research approaches that support compliance with the EU Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542.
During a subsequent tour of the “FFB PreFab” in Münster-Amelsbüren, the delegation gained insights into the research infrastructure for industry-oriented battery cell production. The “FFB PreFab” provides a testing facility equipped with state-of-the-art European plant technology for the joint activities, enabling novel cell concepts and production technologies to be tested under industry-relevant conditions and prepared for transition to large-scale production. Particularly for the planned research activities in the field of new battery materials as well as cell and production technologies, the research infrastructure offers the opportunity to investigate innovative approaches under real-world conditions and to evaluate their industrial scalability at an early stage.

title: 'It's very counterintuitive': The quantum batteries that upend the rules of charging - Batteries News
content:
‘It’s very counterintuitive’: The quantum batteries that upend the rules of charging
Scientists have made the world’s first quantum battery prototype and, unlike conventional batteries, it charges faster the larger it gets. Could these bizarre devices one day power quantum computing – or even your phone?
Everyone knows that the larger the battery, the longer it takes to charge – that’s why it can take several hours to charge a laptop and typically all night to charge an electric vehicle.
That’s the world we’re familiar with, anyway. But in the world of the very small, different rules apply. Quantum mechanics (the science of matter at atomic and subatomic scales) “sort of flips [that] on its head”, says James Quach, a quantum science researcher at Csiro, Australia’s national science agency.
Quach is working to create a quantum battery that defies common sense by charging faster the bigger it gets. Just as some expect quantum computers to one day revolutionise computing, Quach argues that quantum batteries could be similarly disruptive.
In March 2026, his team made an important breakthrough when they unveiled what they say is the world’s first working quantum battery prototype.
The field is still in its infancy, and quantum technology is inherently tricksy. But some scientists say these batteries could one day power quantum devices, while the strongest advocates insist they could even be used to charge everyday devices like phones.
Others, though, remain strongly sceptical about their real-world viability.
Subverting energy limits
Conventional batteries rely on chemical reactions that send 10 billion billion electrons or more rushing through the device they’re powering. It sounds impressive, but some now see the technology as outdated.
Dario Ferraro,
associate professor of physics at the University of Genova, Italy, says:
Despite major technological improvements, modern batteries still rely on electrochemical processes first explored over two centuries ago,
This has led some researchers to look towards quantum batteries – batteries that are powered by quantum effects, rather than chemical reactions.
The key point is that quantum batteries are not about storing a great amount of energy, but about delivering it faster and with greater control – Dario Ferraro
The world of the very small is an overwhelmingly odd one. And quantum mechanics is no stranger to mind-bending concepts, from “entangled” particles that influence each other at
great distances
time that flows backwards
The research that laid the groundwork for quantum batteries was
initially driven
quantum batteries might charge – and discharge – more efficiently
than conventional ones.
Ferraro,
The key point is that quantum batteries are not about storing a great amount of energy, but about delivering it faster and with greater control,
A new prototype
Quach has tested one way of harnessing these quantum effects to power a battery.
He uses an optical microcavity, an experimental set-up where two tiny mirrors are placed 100nm apart (a width about a thousand times thinner than a human hair). He fills the tiny space between the mirrors with organic dye molecules, then beams in a laser.
Using this method, the light and the molecules become strongly coupled, forming hybrid light-matter states, which enhances the system’s ability to absorb and store energy – an effect known as superabsorption.
It’s superabsorption that’s responsible for the battery’s most surprising property. In classical physics, molecules are little individualists – each acting on its own and absorbing energy at a rate independent of the molecules around it. But with quantum effects, they’re a little more collectivist: they “act in unison and synergise”, s
So that the rate at which you can absorb energy increases with the number of molecules there are.
It means that the more molecules there are (i.e. the bigger the battery) the faster it charges. Quach’s prototype took femtoseconds (quadrillionths of a second) to charge, and stored the energy for nanoseconds, about six orders of magnitudes longer.
This feat was first demonstrated by Quach and his team in 2022. In March 2026, they added a new layer, managing to extract an electrical current from the prototype. At greater intensities, this current could potentially be used to charge devices.
Quach’s optical microcavity method isn’t the only way to make a quantum battery. Another approach, for example, uses superconductive materials – already widely used in quantum computing.
One big advantage of Quach’s design, though, is that it works at room temperature. Superconductive designs only work at cryogenic temperatures starting below -150C (-238F).
This is fine for quantum computers, but not so useful to power your mobile phone,
Mauro Paternostro,
a quantum physicist at Queen’s University Belfast, says:
If the goal is proving the quantum charging advantage as real physics… the optical microcavity route is the strongest bet,
But in the long term, Paternostro believes that the superconductive design might have the edge for practical uses, because it is easier to extract energy from. “A microcavity gives you a beautiful ensemble demonstration, but poor control over getting the energy back out in a useful, directed form.”
A delicate state
Quach’s latest experiment represents a first tentative step towards a quantum battery that could one day be substituted for conventional ones. However, at present, the prototype battery can only hold a very small amount of energy – a few billion electron volts – for a matter of nanoseconds. To power conventional devices, it would need to store far more energy for far longer.
Quach says he has in fact already achieved this with a new design he’s built, and is now working on a paper to publish the results. It uses “a hybrid structure”, he says, involving quantum components to allow super-fast charging with classical layers added in to store the energy for longer.
He also plans to combine many microscopic quantum batteries together to increase their total capacity.
If we do those two things, then we’re on our way to be able to power a conventional device,
Still, other scientists remain sceptical, given quantum effects are notoriously fragile and are easily disrupted by observation or interference. “Interactions with the environment can quickly degrade [quantum] effects, limiting both performance and scalability,” says Ferraro, which could offset part of the expected benefit of quantum batteries. Addressing this is “crucial to moving quantum batteries from theory to real-world applications”, he adds.
A quantum world
Advancements in quantum batteries – if they are ever achieved – will likely impact quantum computing first. Quantum computers promise to one day execute tasks more rapidly than the fastest supercomputers, and technologists have warned
they could threaten encryption globally
Others, though, are more sceptical: a recent paper, for example, named quantum computers alongside fusion energy and brain-computer interfaces as being among the technologies perpetually described as “five years away”.
Quach, however, argues that he is likely to achieve the powering of quantum devices with quantum batteries in his lab within the next few years. If possible, this could reduce the amount of energy quantum computers consume, as well as making them faster and less error-prone, allowing them to be scaled up faster, he claims.
Quach is less certain about using them to power conventional devices. It should one day be viable, he says, noting the fact the battery is charged with a laser means it could potentially “charge electric vehicles on-the-go”. This would avoid the need for drivers to stop to recharge altogether.
Ferraro, however, is sceptical that quantum batteries could ever become the norm outside of quantum applications.
In my view… quantum batteries are unlikely to replace conventional batteries in everyday applications such as mobile phones or electric vehicles,
“Their natural domain is the quantum scale.”
The big unsolved problem right now, says Paternostro, is making use of the quantum charging advantage while also withdrawing the energy in a controlled, usable state. Whoever achieves this, he says, “will have made the real breakthrough”.

, a French deep-tech company specializing in green engineering of materials for energy applications, announces that it delivered to the
French Army Technical Section
(“STAT”), in the third quarter of 2026, a first batch of prototype batteries intended for tactical radio sets. Using its high-capacity cells, Novacium designed batteries offering twice the energy capacity of the batteries currently in service.
This delivery follows the award,
at the end of June 2026
, of a contract by STAT to develop and supply, in successive batches, these high-capacity prototype batteries.
Transition to 21700 Cells: Double the Capacity While Preserving Compatibility
To achieve this objective, Novacium integrated GEN3 21700 cylindrical cells in place of the previously used 18650 cells. This format offers higher capacity but integrating it required preserving compatibility with existing equipment. Through an optimized cell arrangement and adapted enclosure geometry, Novacium’s teams limited dimensional changes to meet STAT’s dimensional and connector requirements while doubling the battery’s energy capacity. A patent application has been filed for this design.
Through the integration of these 21700 cells, the new battery pack reaches an onboard energy capacity of 144 Wh, twice the 72 Wh of the reference battery currently in service, and an energy density of 261 Wh/kg, compared with 160 Wh/kg for the existing solution, representing a 63% increase.
An adapted battery management system (BMS), combined with this patent-pending enclosure assembly system, makes the new battery fully compatible with existing connectors, chargers, and interfaces, with only minor changes to its dimensions and mass (42.6 × 98.63 × 74.35 mm; 551 g).
Under a comparable usage profile, this doubled energy capacity is
intended
to provide up to twice the operating time of the reference battery while
retaining
existing connectors and chargers. STAT will evaluate the operating time actually achieved under operational conditions.
An Evaluation Campaign and User Feedback Expected in the Coming Weeks
The first batch of prototype batteries delivered in the third quarter of 2026 will undergo an evaluation campaign under operational conditions conducted by STAT. At the end of this phase, detailed feedback (RETEX) will be prepared jointly by STAT and Novacium in the coming weeks. Lessons learned from this field evaluation will allow Novacium to make the necessary design, ergonomic, and parameter-setting adjustments before producing and delivering a second batch that better reflects a production configuration.
Dr. Jed Kraiem,
Ph.D., Chief Operating Officer of Novacium, said:
Doubling the onboard energy of a tactical radio battery while retaining the existing connectors and chargers represented an engineering challenge that our teams successfully addressed.
”The transition to 21700 cells enabled us to double the battery’s energy capacity, and we worked to limit geometric modifications to preserve compatibility with equipment currently in service. The delivery of this first batch for evaluation under operational conditions is a key milestone: user feedback will guide the adjustments to be made before production of the second batch,”
Bernard Tourillon
, President and CEO of HPQ Silicon Inc., which is itself President of Novacium, said:
The delivery of this first batch illustrates Novacium’s ability to transform its anode-material expertise into batteries designed for critical applications,
“If the evaluation phase confirms the expected performance, this program could provide a technical basis for offering the solution to other allied forces with comparable requirements. For HPQ, this program also illustrates the strategic value of our 36.8% interest in Novacium and of its activities in the defence sector.”
Next Step: A Second Batch Representative of a Production Configuration
Following the evaluation campaign and RETEX, Novacium will begin production of a second batch of batteries incorporating lessons learned in the field and better representing a production configuration. This second batch will integrate Novacium’s new GEN4 cells, with a capacity exceeding 6,500 mAh, with the objective of increasing the battery’s energy capacity at the same mass and therefore its energy density and potential operating time. This stage aims to evaluate the solution’s robustness, ergonomics, and reproducibility for potential larger-scale deployment.
This first delivery forms part of the expansion of Novacium’s activities in the defence and autonomous-systems sectors, notably including the order for battery packs intended for French Army drones, announced on
August 19, 2026
through LN’INNOV, and the order for 100 drone battery packs from Alta Ares announced on
September 17, 2026

Battery fires at recycling centres are costing UK £1bn a year, figures show
Experts say fires caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those in vapes, are putting lives at risk
Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries such as those found in vapes are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to new figures.
Experts say the sheer volume of battery fires now occurring at waste facilities has reached a crisis that is putting lives at risk, costing £1bn a year and frustrating fire chiefs.
In figures shared with the Guardian, the Environment Services Association (ESA), the trade body for waste management companies, said its members had reported 1,518 fires in the year to March 2026. At least 541 of these fires were directly attributed to lithium ion batteries, the survey found. There were a further 216 battery fires in bin lorries.
The ESA said the reported number of battery-related fires underestimated the scale of the problem, because in most incidents it was impossible to determine the cause of the blaze.
A spokesperson
We know 40% of fires at recycling centres are caused by batteries, but we think the actual number is more like 70%.
It estimates that annual cost of these fires has increased from £150m in 2021 to £1bn today. The cause of this week’s blaze at a recycling centre in Deptford, south-east London, has yet to be determined. It was the latest in a series of fires at recycling centre and bin lorries, many of which have been blamed on batteries, particularly those in vapes. They include: Ilford in east London; Caerwent in Monmouthshire; Widnes in Cheshire; Glasgow; Costessey near Norwich, and Dereham in Norfolk.
Fire chiefs have been alarmed by the rise in this type of blaze and the resources needed to put them out.
After the Ilford fire,
which took 25 firefighters to control, a spokesperson for London fire brigade said:
We’ve seen a growing number of fires at waste disposal sites that are believed to have been caused by a lithium battery.
“Fires that we attend at sites like recycling centres and scrap yards can be very time consuming for our firefighters and often require a high level of resources to put the fire out. We’ve also seen the detrimental environmental and societal impact these fires can have on local communities.”
Dr Francesco Restuccia,
a fire expert at King’s College London, said:
There has been exponential increase in fires at recycling centres, mainly because we are using and discarding lithium batteries in everyday objects like smartphones, children’s toys, toothbrushes and vapes.
”If they are not disposed off properly there’s a high chance of ignition.”
Explaining what happens when a lithium battery gets crushed,
Restuccia
If the separator is pierced – which happens a lot at recycling centres – it creates a lot of internal short circuits in the battery, causing the temperature to increase until it reaches ignition point.
The ESA commissioned the Health and Safety Executive to test what happens when a vape battery is punctured while next to paper and card. Video of the experiment, shared with the Guardian, showed the vape igniting like a sparkler and setting alight the paper and card. Temperatures of the vape reached more 750C in the experiment and became hot enough to ignite paper for two minutes.
The ESA hopes the experiment will demonstrate the need to safely dispose vapes to policymakers and the public. The waste management company Biffa said it has recovered 500,000 vapes at its facilities this summer alone.
The ESA is calling for a £5 deposit scheme on the sale of all vapes to ensure that vape users have an incentive to return used devices to retailers for safe disposal.
Patrick Brighty,
the head of recycling policy at the ESA, said:
Battery fires are reaching epidemic proportions across Britain’s recycling and waste industry, placing workers at risk and threatening vital infrastructure upon which we all rely every day.
“It only takes a single battery hidden in household rubbish or recycling to cause a huge fire and decimate a facility. The total cost of battery fires now exceeds £1bn a year, with huge knock-on implications for insurance costs.Vapes are among the biggest culprits because they’re cheap, abundant and typically have a short use-life. ESA and others across our industry are calling on the government to implement a mandatory deposit scheme for vapes to incentivise users to return them safely back to the point of purchase so they can be recycled properly and away from other waste.”

Europe’s Largest NING SERVICE Experience Center Opens in Norway – Full-lifecycle battery services
OSLO, Norway, Sept. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — On 24 September 2026, CATL opened its largest NING SERVICE centre outside Asia in Oslo, extending its battery lifecycle service network in Europe.
The 8,000 square metre centre will serve Norway and the wider Nordic region, providing battery services, training local technicians and supporting circular economy efforts across the region.
Norway is one of the world’s most advanced EV markets. In August, battery electric vehicles made up 98.7% of new passenger car registrations, and electric buses accounted for more than 60% of bus and coach registrations. As this fleet grows and ages, demand for battery diagnostics, repair and life extension is rising. The Norway Centre is built to meet it.
Full-lifecycle battery services
Drawing on CATL’s R&D and manufacturing expertise, NING SERVICE covers the full battery lifecycle: testing, maintenance, repair, insurance, second life and recycling. Its services span transport, energy storage and robotics.
NING SERVICE is helping shift the aftermarket from replacing batteries to repairing them, and has cut turnaround for complex repairs from 72 to 48 hours.
Its deep repair capability covers 76.8% of EV models and applies CATL’s production-line quality standards. The Intelligent Eagle Eye System, used in more than 150 repair facilities, provides full traceability and quality control.
The centre will also serve as a brand experience space and sales agent for emerging electric applications, including vessels, eVTOL aircraft and robotics. NING SERVICE already manages agency sales for CATL’s ecosystem partners, such as AutoFlight and Galbot.
Circularity and local skills
CATL launched the Global Energy Circularity Commitment (GECC) in strategic partnership with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. In line with its vision, NING SERVICE is building an aftermarket ecosystem that keeps batteries in use for longer and returns their materials into new batteries.
Miranda Schnitger,
Climate Lead at the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, said:
In a circular economy, batteries stay in use at their highest value for as long as possible, and their materials are recovered to make new ones.
Inspection, maintenance and repair services are an important part of making that happen at scale,
The centre will create skilled green jobs and become NING SERVICE’s main training hub in the Nordics. Drawing on a training network across 39 European countries and a team of 14 experienced instructors, it will offer courses certified by CATL and practical training for local technicians. NING SERVICE also plans to work more closely with Norwegian universities and technical institutions to build local expertise.
Bringing service closer to customers
CATL is expanding its local presence worldwide through local infrastructure and ecosystem partnerships. The Norway Centre will be a key hub in NING SERVICE’s European network, bringing high-quality service closer to customers in line with its promise to be “Your Nearby New Energy Service Expert.”
Benedikt G. Gudmundsson,
Founder and Chairman of YES-EU Group, said:
CATL brings technology, industry expertise and a trusted brand.
”Combined with YES-EU’s local knowledge and service capabilities, we can build a stronger battery service ecosystem across the Nordics and support the long-term growth of Europe’s EV market.
Bruce Li,
President of Quality Systems, Aftermarket Business Division, CATL, said:
Customers are at the heart of everything we do at NING SERVICE. Working closely with our local partners, we will provide reliable battery lifecycle services that meet the needs of Norway’s EV market and support its continued electrification,
NING SERVICE operates 1,394 service locations across 85 countries and regions. It aims to reach 100 countries and regions by 2027 and 10,000 service locations by 2030.

Pye-Barker Fire & Safety Marks Fire Prevention Week with Lithium-Ion Battery Guidance for Commercial Facilities
ATLANTA, Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — In observance of Fire Prevention Week (Oct. 4-10), Pye-Barker Fire & Safety, the largest fully integrated and full-service fire protection, life safety and security services provider in the United States, is sharing lithium-ion battery safety guidance for commercial facility managers. This year’s National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) theme, “Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” marks the second year the campaign has focused on lithium-ion batteries.
NFPA’s campaign centers on everyday charging habits. Pye-Barker is extending that message to the workplace, where lithium-ion batteries power backup systems for servers and network equipment, forklifts, cordless tools, and the e-bikes and scooters employees and tenants bring inside.
Joseph Hightower,
chief operations officer of Pye-Barker Fire & Safety, said:
Our technicians are finding UPS systems, charging carts and personal e-bikes in rooms that were never designed for them,
“Detection and suppression have to match what is in the space today.”
Pye-Barker recommends five steps:
Inventory and check code.
Walk your building and write down every place a battery is stored, charged or installed, then check that list against what your fire protection plan actually covers.
Buy listed, charge as intended.
Choose equipment certified by a nationally recognized testing laboratory and use only the manufacturer’s charger or an approved equivalent.
Dedicate a supervised charging space.
Use noncombustible surfaces away from exits and stairwells; plug into receptacles rather than extension cords or power strips. Prohibit overnight charging.
Match detection and suppression to the hazard.
Failing cells vent flammable gas before smoke or flame. Battery rooms need early-warning detection tied to a monitored alarm, ventilation and a suppression approach evaluated for the installation.
Train for warning signs.
Heat, swelling, hissing, odor or smoke means stop using the battery. Pye-Barker’s local teams can walk a facility with its building manager and recommend detection, suppression and inspection steps for the site. To reach your local branch, visit pyebarkerfs.com/locations.

title: Battery Show: Ford, GM Pivot to Grid Energy Storage
content:
Market Analysis
Automotive & Mobility
Stationary Batteries
Battery Manufacturing
Interviews
As EV demand stabilizes, Ford and GM are converting battery assets to address grid energy storage needs, a trend Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's Ted Miller will explore in his Battery Show keynote.
October 7, 2026
4 Min Read
PNNL's Grid Storage Launchpad
A tempering of the EV market has helped automakers and energy storage providers meet rising grid energy storage demand in the US—but more work remains to stay ahead of the curve. That includes finding domestic alternatives to Li-ion batteries.
That’s the expert perspective of Ted Miller, senior principal advisor for batteries and energy storage at
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory
(PNNL) based in Richmond, Washington.
Miller will share the next steps in progress to meet continued energy storage demand in his keynote “From Concept to Commercialization: Bridging the Domestic Battery Gap” at Informa’s
Battery Show North America
in Detroit from Oct. 12-15.
Ted Miller, senior principal advisor for batteries and energy storage at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Credit: PNNL
EV market slowdown creates grid storage opportunity
Estimated Li-Ion battery demand for 2026 is nearly 1.5TWh for electric vehicles and almost 500GWh for stationary grid energy storage, he noted. While the outlook during the next decade anticipates growth in the EV and the stationary energy storage market, forecasts generally expect the EV market to dominate battery demand.
Related:
Data Centers Highlight AI-Related Sessions at The Battery Show
“Global battery supply is thus far meeting the demand. In some respect, a tempering of the EV market has been beneficial in meeting rising grid energy storage demand. Ford, GM, Volkswagen and other automakers have answered the call to action by converting existing EV battery manufacturing assets to address pressing grid energy storage needs.”
Miller will spotlight current efforts to create the scaleup and validation road map to meet demands for both segments.
PNNL's $75M Grid Storage Launchpad
“The Department of Energy Office of Electricity invested $75M at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory to create the Grid Storage Launchpad, a 93,000-square-foot facility to scale up and validate energy storage technology. GSL has extensive energy storage testing capability as well as advanced characterization technology and pilot prototyping, including a new prismatic cell production line. GSL supports more than 200 staff across PNNL working on energy storage and 90 ongoing projects.”
PNNL's new prismatic cell production line. Credit: PNNL
The Li-ion dilemma: Flexibility vs. critical material dependence
A key challenge to building an energy storage approach that satisfies both legs of this demand for renewable energy is developing and proving out new battery technologies. Miller noted that though there are many potential options for stationary grid energy storage — for instance, sodium-ion and flow batteries — Li-ion batteries “are the preferred choice for EVs and grid energy storage due to their demonstrated reliability and affordability.
Related:
Battery Makers Pivot from EV to Grid Storage, Defense & AI as Demand Landscape Changes
“The good news is that Li-ion technology has proven extremely flexible and suited to a range of applications and power and energy demands. The bad news is that Li-ion’s success has placed increasing demand on critical materials. Lack of U.S. domestic availability and processing at scale of some materials used in Li-ion batteries also contributes to concern. Developing and validating domestic alternatives to Li-ion batteries for grid energy storage may be one of the keys to growing both markets.”
Bridging the concept-to-commercialization gap
Another critical element to meeting domestic energy storage demand will be partnerships between industry and national labs to accelerate energy storage technology development and validation for domestic production at scale, Miller continued.
“The Department of Energy Office of Electricity and Transportation Technology Office have supported domestic battery research and development, including such organizations aa the United States Advanced Battery Consortium. The result has been development of battery technology used in Ford, GM and Stellantis electrified vehicles. The DOE has also supported battery materials development and testing at the national laboratories.
“What has been missing is the link from concept to commercialization. PNNL aims to bridge that gap by partnering with industry and employing facilities such as GSL to validate energy storage technology for domestic production.”
Related:

How automaker expertise can transform grid energy storage
Miller will also address how the know-how of top US automakers Ford and GM can be leveraged to influence buildout of a robust domestic energy storage ecosystem.
“They can establish a new standard of design and validation process efficiency for grid energy storage systems,” he advised. “Lessons learned in the development of battery cell and system technology for automotive applications will inform stationary energy storage system designs.

“Conversely, as they grow their expertise in grid energy storage, those learnings can be applied to future mobile battery designs. Automakers have a compulsive and natural concern about ensuring battery safety. Similar concerns exist with grid energy storage systems and leveraging automotive industry best practices will enhance reliability and could even lower total system cost.”
Validation standards: Lessons from the USABC model
Validating complete energy storage systems and subsystems such as DC blocks is a critical step.
“The USABC played a key role in the early days of electric vehicles to establish standards and performance and safety measures. This again is where PNNL and other national laboratory partners can assist by collaborating on energy storage standards and test procedure development, as well as facilities and personnel to conduct the validation.”

title: Honeywell battery tech catches hidden defects
content:
Testing & Safety
Stationary Batteries
Automotive & Mobility
Battery News
The system uses electrochemical testing and ultrasound to inspect every cell, identifying problems that could cause failures or safety issues later.
October 7, 2026
3 Min Read
Inbound cell recieving solution diagram
Honeyell
Honeywell Technologies
will feature its recently launched Autonomous Cell Finishing technology at The Battery Show North America. Autonomous Cell Finishing (ACF) is designed for incoming inspection of battery cells. These battery evaluations are targeted for pack and module manufacturers producing EVs, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and space, aerospace, and defense applications.
With the Autonomous Cell Finishing solution, Honeywell can answer the question, "If a globally supplied cell is labeled as 'good,' is it really defect-free?" The solution is designed to save battery modules and packs from utilizing defective cells. One defective cell can cause module and pack imbalance, degradation, warranty claims, and even safety issues.
Detecting latent battery defects before production
There's a particular danger from latent defects, explains Alec Falzone, Battery Industry Leader – North America, Honeywell Technologies. "Batteries expand and contract over their life cycle. And when you have a very small out-of-spec situation, it becomes worse over time as things expand and contract."
Related:
Advanced Battery Safety and Testing with ARC Technology
Alec Falzone, Battery Industry Leader – North America, Honeywell Technologies. Credit: Honeywell
Latent defects can include contaminants, separator misalignment, and other issues that can show up with vibration, temperature, fast-charging, and other uses, Falzone said.
The core of the solution is high-speed, 100% in-line inspection and evaluations utilizing electrical, electrochemical, and 3D internal ultrasound characterization to thoroughly check every battery.
Three-pronged battery cell inspection technology
The first "leg of the stool" is electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), according to Falzone.
"Historically, it takes a long time to get a full-sweep EIS of good quality. However, with Honeywell's system, you can do every cell doing a multi-frequency sweep."
The second leg of the stool is looking at parasitic current, he said. "A cell may have a micro-short that's not a complete short circuit. When you short circuit [completely], your voltage goes to zero. But let's say there's metal particulates or electrode overhang where there's contact, but not enough to cause a safety event. There will still be parasitic current, but it's very small. We hold the voltage constant and measure current, and are able to extrapolate and identify problem cells very quickly."
The final leg of the stool is ultrasound inspection. "Working with our partner at Titan AES, we deploy their proprietary ultrasound technology—a non-destructive way to look inside the cell."
And the objective is to look at every cell, he said. "Not just one percent or 10% of the population, but every cell."
Related:
Battery Safety Testing and Monitoring Methods Explained
Honeywell then utilizes intelligent methods that enable closed-loop defect identification for removal of bad cells and provide real-time upstream feedback and resolution.
This is all orchestrated by Honeywell's Battery Manufacturing Excellence Platform (Battery-MXP). This system is fast, efficient, and not only catches obvious problems, but also identifies those latent defects. The platform also provides insights into the cycle-life of individual cells.
Honeywell's solution is able to catch these latent defects and provide what the company terms "Informative Defect Identification" to return the cells and provide feedback to the supplier for corrective action and preventative action (CAPA). This not only helps the pack and module manufacturer, but also helps the global battery supplier address issues for better future product and implement cost savings by reducing scrap costs.
